title: The bomber built for Japan

facts.text: The B-29 began with a 1940 Army Air Corps demand for a bomber that could fly 400 mph and travel 5,000 miles. Boeing's answer, the Model 345, first flew on 21 September 1942.
Gen. Henry H. Arnold believed in it so strongly that the Army ordered 1,500 before the first prototype had flown.
It was the first bomber with pressurized crew areas.
Its guns sat in remote controlled turrets. An analog computer fire control system let gunners at sighting stations aim turrets they were not sitting in.
Four 2,200 horsepower Wright R-3350 radial engines gave it a top speed of 357 mph, with a wingspan of 141 feet 3 inches.
In December 1943 American leaders decided not to send it to Europe but to use its range against Japan. The first B-29 raids on Japan came from China on 15 June 1944.
On 24 November 1944, 111 B-29s took off from Saipan for the first raid on Tokyo from the Marianas. At 27,000 to 33,000 feet they met winds of about 120 knots, and only 24 bombed the target.
From March 1945 Curtis LeMay sent them in low, at night, with incendiaries. On 6 and 9 August 1945 B-29s dropped the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. In all, 3,970 were built.

declassified.fact: Past its prime, the B-29 went back to war five years later. In Korea B-29s flew about 20,000 sorties, dropped about 200,000 tons of bombs, and their gunners shot down 27 enemy aircraft.

film.record: 18-CS-3338, Saipan Harbor and Airfield; B-29 Takeoffs and Landings (NARA 4878)
film.shot_notes: AAF Combat Subjects reel, two reels joined, silent (the WMV audio track is only hiss), converted to H.264, 17 min 11 s. 00:00 to 03:00 Saipan harbor, LSTs and the coast (not used). 03:15 to 05:40 dark night shots, lights only (avoid). 05:45 to 06:20 a B-29 high overhead. Slates at 06:52 and 07:58 read "Locantore Roll 4 (and 5), B-29s Return 3/4/45". 7 P.M.: open at 08:04 on a B-29 low over the runway, wheels down, sweeping past the camera (08:00 to 08:16), then the taxiing B-29 close past the camera 07:18 to 07:32 or the rows of parked B-29s 07:34 to 07:56. More landings 08:28 to 08:40, a close pass 08:50 to 08:52 and 09:00; reel 2 (from 09:00 slate) has more landings 12:00 to 13:30 and ground crew under a B-29 14:15 to 14:50. Different film from the noon video (No. 086 uses 18-CS-3655), so no shot repeats.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Army Air Forces, NARA Record Group 18, Army Air Forces Combat Subjects). NARA use status 'Undetermined', the routine flag on these reels.
film.date_note: Filmed 4 March 1945 per the camera slates (B-29s returning from a mission), not on 24 November 1944. The caption should say B-29s landing on Saipan, March 1945.

body:
Gen. Henry H. Arnold was so sure of this bomber that the Army ordered 1,500 of them before the prototype had flown.

24 November 1944. 111 B-29s took off from Saipan for Tokyo, the first raid on the Japanese capital from the Marianas. This was the range the plane was built for. It came from a 1940 call for a bomber that could fly 400 mph and travel 5,000 miles, and Boeing's design first flew in September 1942.

Four 2,200 horsepower Wright R-3350 engines gave it 357 mph. In December 1943 American leaders chose to keep it out of Europe and turn it on Japan.

3,970 were built. Two of them dropped the atomic bombs in August 1945.
